title: Physiology of GIT Absorption and Selective Malabsorption

questions.q: The book lists the stages of absorption, in order, as:
questions.exp: Stages of absorption: 1. Luminal, 2. Mucosal, 3. Post mucosal. (Book p6)

questions.q: Match the numbered stage of absorption to its descriptor — 1) Stage 1 2) Stage 2 3) Stage 3 … A) Mucosal B) Post mucosal C) Luminal
questions.exp: Stage 1 = Luminal (enzymes mediated), Stage 2 = Mucosal (small intestinal enterocyte), Stage 3 = Post mucosal (into blood). (Book p6)

questions.q: The luminal stage of absorption is described as:
questions.exp: 1. Luminal: Enzymes mediated. (Book p6)

questions.q: In the mucosal stage the villi ____ contains enzymes.
questions.exp: Mucosal: small intestinal mucosal — enterocyte; villi brush border contains enzymes. (Book p6)

questions.q: The cell type named for the mucosal stage of absorption is the:
questions.exp: 2. Mucosal: small intestinal mucosal — Enterocyte, with brush border enzymes. (Book p6)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the book defines the post mucosal stage as movement from the mucosal epithelial cell into blood.
opts: True — mucosal epithelial cell → into blood
False — post mucosal is transport into lymph
False — post mucosal is the luminal enzyme step
True — but only for short chain fatty acids
questions.exp: 3. Post mucosal: mucosal epithelial cell → into blood. (Book p6)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one of these is not a printed stage of absorption:
questions.exp: The three printed stages are Luminal, Mucosal and Post mucosal; 'post absorptive' is not listed. (Book p6)

questions.q: A toxin selectively destroys the brush-border enzymes of the small intestinal enterocyte. Which stage of absorption is blocked?
questions.exp: Brush border enzymes belong to the enterocyte — i.e. the mucosal stage. (Book p6)

questions.q: How many stages of absorption does the book list?
questions.exp: Three stages: Luminal, Mucosal, Post mucosal. (Book p6)

questions.q: The proximal two-thirds of the small intestine is described as the site of:
opts: Bile acid and vitamin B12 absorption
questions.exp: Proximal (2/3): maximum absorption (Jejunum > Duodenum). (Book p6)

questions.q: Proximal (2/3) of the small intestine shows maximum absorption (____ > Duodenum).
questions.exp: Proximal (2/3): maximum absorption (Jejunum > Duodenum). (Book p6)

questions.q: The distal one-third of the small intestine (ileum) absorbs:
opts: Bile acid, vitamin B12 and Mg2+
questions.exp: Distal (1/3): absorption of bile acid, Vit B12, Mg2+ (ileum). (Book p6)

questions.q: All of the following are absorbed in the distal one-third (ileum) EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Distal (1/3) absorbs bile acid, Vit B12 and Mg2+; iron is absorbed proximally (duodenum > jejunum). (Book p6)

questions.q: Match the small intestinal segment to its printed role — 1) Proximal 2/3 2) Distal 1/3 … A) Bile acid, Vit B12, Mg2+ (ileum) B) Maximum absorption (jejunum > duodenum)
questions.exp: Proximal 2/3 = maximum absorption (jejunum > duodenum); distal 1/3 = bile acid, Vit B12, Mg2+ (ileum). (Book p6)

questions.q: What fraction of the small intestine is described as the proximal segment of maximum absorption?
questions.exp: Proximal (2/3): maximum absorption (Jejunum > Duodenum). (Book p6)

questions.q: The specific feature of the small intestinal mucosa named by the book is:
questions.exp: Enterocyte: villi (specific feature). (Book p6)

questions.q: Villi are surrounded by crypts of ____.
questions.exp: Villi (specific feature) are surrounded by crypts of Lieberkühn. (Book p6)

questions.q: The villi contain a:
questions.exp: Enterocyte villi contain the brush border. (Book p6)

questions.q: Paneth cells are located:
opts: At the base of the crypts
questions.exp: Crypts: Paneth cells (at base). (Book p6)

questions.q: Paneth cells produce immunological substances, namely:
questions.exp: Paneth cells (at base) produce immunological substances: alpha defensins, lysozymes, phospholipase A2. (Book p6)

questions.q: All of the following are listed Paneth-cell products EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Paneth cells produce alpha defensins, lysozymes and phospholipase A2; mucus comes from goblet cells. (Book p6)

questions.q: Besides Paneth cells, the crypts contain:
questions.exp: Crypts: Paneth cells (at base), enteroendocrine cells, goblet cells. (Book p6)

questions.q: Small intestinal epithelium shows continuous renewal every:
questions.exp: Continuous renewal: every 48-72 hrs. (Book p6)

questions.q: The lamina propria of the small intestinal mucosa contains:
questions.exp: b. Lamina propria: glands, blood vessels. (Book p6)

questions.q: The muscularis mucosa of the small intestine is described as having:
questions.exp: c. Muscularis mucosa: tight attachment. (Book p6)

questions.q: Match the mucosal compartment to its printed content — 1) Lamina propria 2) Muscularis mucosa 3) Crypt … A) Paneth cells at base B) Glands, blood vessels C) Tight attachment
questions.exp: Lamina propria = glands, blood vessels; muscularis mucosa = tight attachment; crypts contain Paneth cells at the base. (Book p6)

questions.q: Plica circularis is defined in the note as:
opts: Visible mucosal folds on the luminal surface of the small intestine
The pacemaker cell network of the gut
The smooth muscle coat of the colon
questions.exp: Note: plica circularis — visible mucosal folds on the luminal surface of the small intestine. (Book p6)

questions.q: Interstitial cells of Cajal in the small intestine are:
questions.exp: Interstitial cells of Cajal: pacemaker cells of the small intestine — basal electrical rhythm. (Book p6)

questions.q: Interstitial cells of Cajal generate the ____ of the small intestine.
questions.exp: Interstitial cells of Cajal: pacemaker cells of the small intestine → basal electrical rhythm. (Book p6)

questions.q: Peyer's patches are located in the:
questions.exp: 2. Submucosa: Peyer's patches (in ileum). (Book p7)

questions.q: Peyer's patches are described as:
questions.exp: Peyer's patches (in ileum): macroscopic lymphoid aggregates. (Book p7)

questions.q: At ileocolonoscopy a surgeon notes hypertrophied Peyer's patches. The book links this hypertrophy to:
questions.exp: Peyer's patches (in ileum): in typhoid — hypertrophy. (Book p7)

questions.q: Order the small intestinal layers as printed (innermost → outermost) — 1) Mucosa 2) Submucosa 3) Muscularis propria 4) Serosa … A) Serosa B) Mucosa C) Submucosa D) Muscularis propria
questions.exp: Histology layers: 1. mucosa, 2. submucosa, 3. muscularis propria, 4. serosa. (Book p7)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not a printed layer of the small intestine:
questions.exp: The printed layers are mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria and serosa; adventitia is not listed. (Book p7)

questions.q: The luminal phase of fat absorption requires:
questions.exp: Luminal phase mechanism: bile acids + pancreatic lipase act on triglyceride. (Book p7)

questions.q: Pancreatic lipase acts on triglyceride (TGA) by the process of ____.
questions.exp: TGA → lipolysis (by pancreatic lipase) → fatty acids + glycerol. (Book p7)

questions.q: Lipolysis of triglyceride in the lumen yields:
questions.exp: Lipolysis of TGA gives fatty acids + glycerol. (Book p7)

questions.q: Order the luminal fat steps as printed — 1) TGA 2) Lipolysis 3) Fatty acids + glycerol … A) Fatty acids + glycerol B) TGA C) Lipolysis
questions.exp: Bile acids + pancreatic lipase act on TGA → lipolysis → fatty acids + glycerol. (Book p7)

questions.q: A patient with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhea. The book attributes this to loss of:
questions.exp: Defects in luminal absorption: 1. chronic pancreatitis → affects pancreatic lipase → lipolysis affected. (Book p7)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the book shows micelles entering enterocytes by passive diffusion in the luminal phase.
opts: True — passive diffusion of micelles into enterocytes
False — uptake is active via SGLT1
False — micelles are excluded from enterocytes
True — but only for short chain fatty acids
questions.exp: Micelle → passive diffusion into enterocytes. (Book p7)

questions.q: The bile acid body pool is:
questions.exp: Bile acid physiology: body pool 4 g (maintained by enterohepatic circulation). (Book p7)

questions.q: The bile acid body pool is maintained by the ____ circulation.
questions.exp: Body pool: 4 g (maintained by enterohepatic circulation). (Book p7)

questions.q: The rate-limiting enzyme of bile acid synthesis is:
questions.exp: Synthesis: 7α-hydroxylase is the rate limiting step. (Book p7)

questions.q: The primary bile acids formed by synthesis are:
questions.exp: Synthesis produces cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid. (Book p7)

questions.q: Bile acids are conjugated with:
questions.exp: Conjugation with glycine/taurine. (Book p7)

questions.q: After conjugation, bile acids are termed:
questions.exp: Conjugation (glycine/taurine) → bile salts. (Book p7)

questions.q: Bacterial deconjugation in the colon produces:
questions.exp: Colon: bacterial deconjugation → deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid. (Book p7)

questions.q: Match the enterohepatic step to its printed product — 1) Synthesis (rate limiting) 2) Conjugation 3) Colonic bacterial deconjugation … A) Glycine/taurine → bile salts B) 7α-hydroxylase → cholic & chenodeoxycholic acid C) Deoxycholic & lithocholic acid
questions.exp: Synthesis (7α-hydroxylase, rate limiting) → cholic/chenodeoxycholic acid; conjugation with glycine/taurine → bile salts; colonic bacterial deconjugation → deoxycholic and lithocholic acid. (Book p7)

questions.q: Reabsorbed bile acids return to the liver through the:
questions.exp: Bile salts are reabsorbed and returned via the portal circulation to the liver. (Book p7)

questions.q: After ileal resection a patient develops bile-acid diarrhea. The enterohepatic step lost is:
questions.exp: Ileal disease removes the reabsorption limb of the enterohepatic circulation. (Book p7)

questions.q: Chronic pancreatitis causes a luminal defect by affecting:
opts: Pancreatic lipase, so lipolysis is affected
questions.exp: 1. Chronic pancreatitis → affects pancreatic lipase → lipolysis affected. (Book p8)

questions.q: The book's 'bile acid defect' may be a defect in:
questions.exp: 2. Bile acid defect: defect in secretion / synthesis / reabsorption. (Book p8)

questions.q: Match the bile acid defect to the printed cause — 1) Destruction of bile ducts 2) Ileal dysfunction 3) Early deconjugation in the small intestine … A) TB/Crohn's B) Cirrhosis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis C) SIBO
questions.exp: Secretion/synthesis defects: cirrhosis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis (destruction of bile ducts); reabsorption defects: TB/Crohn's (ileal dysfunction) and SIBO (early deconjugation). (Book p8)

questions.q: Early deconjugation of bile acids in the small intestine is listed under:
questions.exp: Defect in reabsorption: small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) — early deconjugation in the small intestine. (Book p8)

questions.q: The mucosal phase of absorption is impaired in:
opts: Coeliac disease, Whipple disease and tropical sprue
questions.exp: Mucosal phase — aetiology: coeliac disease, Whipple disease, tropical sprue. (Book p8)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one of these is not a mucosal phase aetiology in the book:
questions.exp: Mucosal phase: coeliac disease, Whipple disease, tropical sprue. Chronic pancreatitis is a luminal defect. (Book p8)

questions.q: A patient with a duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy has a defect the book places in which phase?
questions.exp: Coeliac disease is listed under the mucosal phase of absorption. (Book p8)

questions.q: Tuberculosis and Crohn's disease produce a bile acid defect by causing:
questions.exp: Defect in reabsorption: TB/Crohn's — ileal dysfunction. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: In the post-mucosal phase, long chain fatty acids and glycerol undergo:
questions.exp: Post mucosal: long chain fatty acids + glycerol → esterification → chylomicrons. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Esterification of long chain fatty acids with glycerol forms:
questions.exp: LCFA + glycerol → esterification → chylomicrons. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Chylomicrons leave the enterocyte by transport via:
questions.exp: Chylomicrons → transport via intestinal lymphatics. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Order the post-mucosal steps — 1) LCFA + glycerol 2) Esterification 3) Chylomicrons 4) Transport via intestinal lymphatics … A) Chylomicrons B) LCFA + glycerol C) Intestinal lymphatics D) Esterification
questions.exp: LCFA + glycerol → esterification → chylomicrons → transport via intestinal lymphatics. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: The two post-mucosal absorption disorders listed are:
questions.exp: Post mucosal: 1. abetalipoproteinaemia, 2. intestinal lymphangiectasia. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Medium chain fatty acids have a carbon chain length of:
questions.exp: Types of fatty acids — carbon chain length: long chain >12, medium chain 8-12, short chain <8. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Short chain fatty acids have a carbon chain length of:
questions.exp: Short chain fatty acids: carbon chain length <8. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Long chain fatty acids have a carbon chain length of:
questions.exp: Long chain fatty acids: carbon chain length >12. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: The primary absorption site of short chain fatty acids is the:
questions.exp: Short chain fatty acids: primary absorption site — colon. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Short chain fatty acids arise from:
opts: Bacterial degradation of unabsorbed carbohydrates in the colon
questions.exp: Short chain fatty acids: origin — bacterial degradation of unabsorbed carbohydrates in the colon. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Medium chain fatty acids are present in small quantity in the diet as:
questions.exp: Medium chain: small quantity in diet (coconut oil). (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Long chain fatty acids are present in the diet in large quantity as:
questions.exp: Long chain: large quantity in diet as triglycerides. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — medium chain fatty acids require pancreatic lipolysis for absorption.
opts: False — they require bile acid conjugation instead
questions.exp: Require pancreatic lipolysis: long chain — yes; medium chain — no; short chain — no. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — short chain fatty acids require micelle formation for absorption.
questions.exp: Require micelle formation: long chain — yes; medium chain — no; short chain — no. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Which fatty acid type is present in stool in substantial amount?
questions.exp: Present in stool: long chain — minimal, medium chain — no, short chain — substantial. (Book p8)

questions.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — only one fatty acid class requires BOTH pancreatic lipolysis and micelle formation:
questions.exp: Only long chain fatty acids require pancreatic lipolysis and micelle formation; medium and short chain require neither. (Book p8)

questions.q: Disaccharides are split into monosaccharides by:
opts: Disaccharidases of the small intestinal brush border epithelium
questions.exp: Mechanism of carbohydrate absorption: disaccharides → small intestinal brush border epithelium (disaccharidases) → monosaccharides. (Book p9)

questions.q: The disaccharidases listed in the book are:
questions.exp: Disaccharidases: lactase, maltase, sucrase, trehalase. (Book p9)

questions.q: Lactose is split by ____ into glucose + galactose.
questions.exp: Lactose —(lactase)→ glucose + galactose. (Book p9)

questions.q: Sucrose is split by sucrase into glucose + ____.
questions.exp: Sucrose —(sucrase)→ glucose + fructose. (Book p9)

questions.q: Match the disaccharide to its printed monosaccharide pair — 1) Lactose 2) Sucrose … A) Glucose + fructose B) Glucose + galactose
questions.exp: Lactose → glucose + galactose (lactase); sucrose → glucose + fructose (sucrase). (Book p9)

questions.q: In the gut, glucose and galactose are absorbed through:
questions.exp: Receptors for absorption in the gut: SGLT1 (sodium glucose cotransporter 1) carries glucose and galactose. (Book p9)

questions.q: Fructose is absorbed in the gut through:
questions.exp: In the gut: fructose uses the facilitated transporter GLUT5. (Book p9)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — the book labels SGLT1-mediated uptake of galactose and glucose as active transport.
questions.exp: In the gut: SGLT1 — active transport of galactose and glucose. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the liver, galactose is phosphorylated by ____ to galactose-1-phosphate.
questions.exp: In the liver: galactose + ATP —(galactokinase)→ galactose-1-phosphate + ADP. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the liver, fructose + ATP is converted by ____ into fructose-1-phosphate + ADP.
questions.exp: In the liver: fructose + ATP —(fructokinase)→ fructose-1-phosphate + ADP. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the liver, glucose + ATP is phosphorylated by ____ to glucose-6-phosphate + ADP.
questions.exp: In the liver: glucose + ATP —(glucokinase)→ glucose-6-phosphate + ADP. (Book p9)

questions.q: In the liver, monosaccharides enter the hepatocyte through:
questions.exp: In the liver: glucose transporter (GLUT2) brings monosaccharides into the hepatocyte. (Book p9)

questions.q: An infant has severe diarrhea from birth with glucose and galactose malabsorption but normal fructose handling. The book names this:
questions.exp: Note: SGLT-1 defect → familial glucose-galactose malabsorption syndrome. (Book p9)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one is not a brush-border disaccharidase listed in the book:
questions.exp: Disaccharidases: lactase, maltase, sucrase, trehalase. Galactokinase is a liver enzyme. (Book p9)

questions.q: Congenital defects of carbohydrate absorption are described as:
questions.exp: Defects in carbohydrate absorption — congenital: autosomal recessive. (Book p9)

questions.q: Match the pattern of carbohydrate malabsorption to the printed example — 1) Selective 2) Global … A) Small intestinal mucosal defect (coeliac, Whipple's, tropical sprue) B) Lactase deficiency (primary/secondary)
questions.exp: Selective = lactase deficiency (primary/secondary); global = small intestinal mucosal defect (coeliac disease, Whipple's disease, tropical sprue). (Book p9)

questions.q: All of the following cause global carbohydrate malabsorption EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Global (small intestinal mucosal defect): coeliac disease, Whipple's disease, tropical sprue. Lactase deficiency is selective. (Book p9)

questions.q: The most common (m/c) acquired lactase deficiency is:
questions.exp: Acquired: ↓ enzyme activity — primary (m/c): genetic defect (allele persistence). (Book p10)

questions.q: Secondary lactase deficiency is listed with:
questions.exp: Lactase deficiency, secondary: infections, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). (Book p10)

questions.q: Trypsinogen is converted to ____, which activates chymotrypsin and elastase.
questions.exp: Mechanism of protein absorption: trypsinogen → trypsin → activates chymotrypsin and elastase. (Book p10)

questions.q: Trypsin activates:
questions.exp: Trypsinogen → trypsin → activate chymotrypsin and elastase. (Book p10)

questions.q: Enterokinase deficiency is listed as a cause of:
questions.exp: Defects in protein absorption — selective malabsorption: enterokinase deficiency. (Book p10)

questions.q: Neutral amino acid transport defect produces:
questions.exp: Neutral amino acid transport defect → Hartnup's disease. (Book p10)

questions.q: Hartnup's disease presents as pellagra with:
questions.exp: Hartnup's disease: presents as pellagra — diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia. (Book p10)

questions.q: Dibasic amino acid transport defect causes:
questions.exp: Dibasic amino acid transport defect → cystinuria. (Book p10)

questions.q: Cystinuria causes excretion of COLA — cystine, ornithine, lysine and ____.
questions.exp: Cystinuria → excretion of COLA (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine). (Book p10)

questions.q: Match the selective protein defect to its printed consequence — 1) Hartnup's disease 2) Cystinuria … A) Excretion of COLA B) Pellagra: diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia
questions.exp: Hartnup's disease → pellagra (diarrhoea, dermatitis, dementia); cystinuria → excretion of COLA. (Book p10)

questions.q: All of the following are in the COLA group excreted in cystinuria EXCEPT:
questions.exp: COLA = cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine; histidine is not included. (Book p10)

questions.q: The dietary sources of lactose named in the book are:
questions.exp: Physiology: lactose (dietary — milk, cheese) → lactase (brush border) → glucose + galactose. (Book p10)

questions.q: Lactase is a ____ enzyme that splits lactose into glucose and galactose.
questions.exp: Lactase is a brush border enzyme: lactose → glucose + galactose. (Book p10)

questions.q: Congenital lactase deficiency is:
opts: Autosomal recessive with absent enzyme from birth
questions.exp: Congenital: autosomal recessive (absent enzyme from birth). (Book p10)

questions.q: Acquired lactase deficiency is characterised by:
questions.exp: Acquired: ↓ enzyme activity. (Book p10)

questions.q: Primary acquired lactase deficiency (m/c) is due to:
questions.exp: Primary (m/c): genetic defect (allele persistence). (Book p10)

questions.q: Secondary lactase deficiency is listed with:
questions.exp: Secondary: infections, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). (Book p10)

questions.q: Order the pathogenesis as printed — 1) Undigested carbohydrate 2) ↑ unabsorbed carbohydrates in colon 3) Fermented by colonic bacteria 4) ↑ acid and gases … A) ↑ acid and gases B) Undigested carbohydrate C) Fermentation by colonic bacteria D) ↑ unabsorbed carbohydrates in colon
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: undigested carbohydrate → ↑ unabsorbed carbohydrates in colon → fermented by colonic bacteria → ↑ acid and gases (H2, methane, CO2). (Book p11)

questions.q: The colonic bacteria listed as fermenting unabsorbed carbohydrate are:
questions.exp: Fermented by colonic bacteria: Bacteroides fragilis, bifidobacteria, lactobacillus. (Book p11)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one organism is not listed among the colonic fermenters of lactose intolerance:
questions.exp: Listed colonic fermenters: Bacteroides fragilis, bifidobacteria, lactobacillus. E. coli is not listed. (Book p11)

questions.q: The gases produced by colonic fermentation are listed as:
questions.exp: ↑ acid and gases (H2, methane, CO2). (Book p11)

questions.q: Symptoms of lactose intolerance appear at what interval after a meal?
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: 90 min post prandial — abdominal distension, bloating, cramps. (Book p11)

questions.q: The 90-minute post-prandial symptoms described are:
questions.exp: 90 min post prandial: abdominal distension, bloating, cramps. (Book p11)

questions.q: Diaper dermatitis in children with lactose intolerance is attributed to:
questions.exp: Diaper dermatitis: in children due to acidic pH. (Book p11)

questions.q: Besides diaper dermatitis, children with lactose intolerance are described with:
opts: Severe watery diarrhea, failure to thrive and irritability
questions.exp: In children: severe watery diarrhea, failure to thrive, irritability. (Book p11)

questions.q: Stool pH in lactose intolerance is:
questions.exp: Investigations: 1. stool pH — acidic. (Book p11)

questions.q: Principle of the lactose hydrogen breath test: excess lactose in colon is fermented by bacteria to methane + H2, which is absorbed and tested on the ____.
questions.exp: Excess lactose in colon → fermented by bacteria → methane + H2 → absorbed → tested on breath. (Book p11)

questions.q: A positive lactose hydrogen breath test is defined as a rise in breath H2 of:
questions.exp: Positive test: H2 > 20 ppm. (Book p11)

questions.q: The lactose-glucose blood test is described as:
questions.exp: 3. Lactose-glucose blood test: obsolete. (Book p11)

questions.q: Management of lactose intolerance in the book is:
questions.exp: Management: dietary management, Ca2+ supplementation. (Book p11)

questions.q: All of the following are listed investigations for lactose intolerance EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Investigations listed: stool pH, lactose hydrogen breath test, lactose-glucose blood test (obsolete). D-xylose is a test of mucosal integrity. (Book p11)

questions.q: A toddler develops abdominal distension and severe watery diarrhea 90 minutes after milk feeds, with acidic perianal dermatitis. The book's diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Lactose intolerance: 90 min post prandial distension, severe watery diarrhea, diaper dermatitis from acidic pH. (Book p11)

questions.q: A child with confirmed lactose intolerance and poor weight gain should be managed by:
opts: Dietary lactose restriction with calcium supplementation
questions.exp: Management: dietary management plus Ca2+ supplementation. (Book p11)

questions.q: The note lists the protein malabsorption mimics as:
opts: Hartnup's disease (similar to pellagra) and cystinuria (COLA excretion)
questions.exp: Note: protein malabsorption — Hartnup's disease: similar to pellagra; cystinuria: excretion of COLA. (Book p11)

questions.q: Abetalipoproteinaemia is also known as:
questions.exp: Abetalipoproteinaemia — AKA neuroacanthocytosis. (Book p12)

questions.q: Inheritance of abetalipoproteinaemia is:
questions.exp: Etiopathogenesis: autosomal recessive. (Book p12)

questions.q: In abetalipoproteinaemia, apoB48 defect causes defective ____, so no chylomicron formation.
questions.exp: apoB48 → defective esterification → no chylomicron formation. (Book p12)

questions.q: Peripheral smear in abetalipoproteinaemia shows:
questions.exp: Investigations: 1. peripheral smear — acanthocytes. (Book p12)

questions.q: Match the components of the printed triad — 1) Neurological 2) Retinopathy 3) GI … A) Steatorrhea B) Ataxia (vitamin E deficiency) C) Retinitis pigmentosa (night blindness)
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: triad of neurological — ataxia (vitamin E deficiency), retinopathy — retinitis pigmentosa (night blindness), GI — steatorrhea. (Book p12)

questions.q: The investigation described as 100% diagnostic for abetalipoproteinaemia is:
questions.exp: 2. Post prandial endoscopic biopsy: 100% diagnostic. (Book p12)

questions.q: The endoscopic biopsy in abetalipoproteinaemia shows:
questions.exp: Post prandial endoscopic biopsy: 100% diagnostic; vacuolation in enterocytes. (Book p12)

questions.q: Match the step in the vitamin E deficiency pathway — 1) ↓ chylomicron formation 2) Fat malabsorption 3) ↓ vitamin E absorption … A) ↓ vitamin E absorption (fat soluble) B) ↓ chylomicron formation C) Fat malabsorption
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: ↓ chylomicron formation → fat malabsorption → ↓ vitamin E absorption (fat soluble). (Book p12)

questions.q: The other limb of vitamin E deficiency in abetalipoproteinaemia is:
opts: ↓ VLDL formation → ↓ secretion of vitamin E by the liver into blood
questions.exp: ↓ VLDL formation → ↓ secretion of vitamin E by the liver into blood. (Book p12)

questions.q: Conditions the book says are diagnosed on biopsy are:
opts: Coeliac disease, tropical sprue and SIBO
Cystinuria, Hartnup disease and enterokinase deficiency
questions.exp: Note: conditions diagnosed with biopsy — Whipple's disease, abetalipoproteinaemia, agammaglobulinaemia. (Book p12)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — hypolipidemia is listed as a clinical feature of abetalipoproteinaemia.
opts: True — but only triglycerides are low
questions.exp: Clinical presentation: hypolipidemia, then the triad of ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa and steatorrhea. (Book p12)

questions.q: A child with steatorrhea, ataxia and night blindness has acanthocytes on smear. The ataxia is most pronounced because of:
questions.exp: Vitamin E deficiency in abetalipoproteinaemia: clinical features — ataxia (pronounced). (Book p12)

questions.q: The physiology box for intestinal lymphangiectasia shows chylomicrons moving:
opts: Across the portal vein into bile
Into the colonic lumen for excretion
questions.exp: Physiology: chylomicrons → across intestinal lymphatics → blood. (Book p13)

questions.q: Secondary intestinal lymphangiectasia follows:
opts: Lymph node obstruction → ↑ lymphatic pressure → exudation
questions.exp: Secondary: lymph node obstruction → ↑ lymphatic pressure → exudation. (Book p13)

questions.q: Secondary causes listed are:
questions.exp: Secondary: lymphoma, Crohn's disease. (Book p13)

questions.q: Primary intestinal lymphangiectasia is described as:
opts: Abnormally dilated lymphatic channels with ↑ pressure and exudation into the intestinal lumen
Obstruction of lymph nodes by metastases
Congenital absence of the thoracic duct
questions.exp: Primary: abnormally dilated lymphatic channel → ↑ pressure → exudation into intestinal lumen. (Book p13)

questions.q: The most important cause of protein losing enteropathy, per the book, is:
questions.exp: 1. Protein losing enteropathy — most important: primary intestinal lymphangiectasia. (Book p13)

questions.q: Protein losing enteropathy produces:
questions.exp: Protein losing enteropathy: hypoalbuminaemia with hypogammaglobulinaemia. (Book p13)

questions.q: Match the cause of edema to the printed mechanism — 1) Nephrotic syndrome 2) Liver disease 3) Protein losing enteropathy … A) ↓ albumin production B) Loss of albumin in urine C) Exudation into the intestinal lumen
questions.exp: Nephrotic syndrome: loss of albumin in urine; liver disease: ↓ albumin production; protein losing enteropathy: exudation into the intestinal lumen. (Book p13)

questions.q: The specific investigation for intestinal lymphangiectasia is:
questions.exp: Investigation: fecal α-1 antitrypsin: elevated (specific test). (Book p13)

questions.q: CT scan in intestinal lymphangiectasia shows:
opts: Wall thickening of the small intestine
questions.exp: CT scan: wall thickening of small intestine. (Book p13)

questions.q: The endoscopic investigation listed for intestinal lymphangiectasia is:
questions.exp: Investigation: video capsule endoscopy. (Book p13)

questions.q: Management of intestinal lymphangiectasia is:
questions.exp: Management: medium chain triglyceride diet. (Book p13)

questions.q: All of the following are listed features of intestinal lymphangiectasia EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Features: protein losing enteropathy with hypoalbuminaemia, edema, ascites, diarrhea. Hyperalbuminaemia is not listed. (Book p13)

questions.q: On endoscopy, intestinal lymphangiectasia appears as:
opts: Diffuse white lesions with dilated lymphatics
questions.exp: Endoscopy image: diffuse white lesions — lymphangiectasia on endoscopy with dilated lymphatics. (Book p13)

units.title: Basics of Absorption & Stages
units.guide:
Three stages in order: Luminal → Mucosal → Post mucosal.
Luminal is enzymes mediated; mucosal is the enterocyte brush border.
Post mucosal is movement from the mucosal epithelial cell into blood.

units.title: Anatomy of the Small Intestine
units.guide:
Proximal 2/3 = maximum absorption (jejunum > duodenum).
Distal 1/3 = bile acid, vitamin B12 and Mg2+ (ileum).
Fix the segment before learning each nutrient.

units.title: Histology: Mucosa
units.guide:
Villi are the specific feature and are surrounded by crypts of Lieberkühn.
Paneth cells sit at the crypt base and make alpha defensins, lysozymes, phospholipase A2.
Renewal every 48-72 hrs; interstitial cells of Cajal are pacemaker cells.

units.title: Small Intestine Layers & Peyer's Patches
units.guide:
Layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis propria, serosa.
Peyer's patches are macroscopic lymphoid aggregates of the ileal submucosa.
In typhoid they hypertrophy.

units.title: Fat Absorption: Luminal Phase
units.guide:
Bile acids + pancreatic lipase act on triglyceride → lipolysis → fatty acids + glycerol.
Micelles then pass into enterocytes by passive diffusion.
Chronic pancreatitis removes the lipase step.

units.title: Bile Acid Physiology
units.guide:
Body pool 4 g, maintained by enterohepatic circulation.
Synthesis (7α-hydroxylase, rate limiting) → cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid → conjugation with glycine/taurine → bile salts.
Colonic bacterial deconjugation gives deoxycholic and lithocholic acid.

units.title: Defects in Luminal & Mucosal Phase
units.guide:
Luminal: chronic pancreatitis (lipase) and bile acid defect (secretion/synthesis/reabsorption).
Bile duct destruction in cirrhosis, PBC, PSC; ileal dysfunction in TB/Crohn's; early deconjugation in SIBO.
Mucosal: coeliac disease, Whipple disease, tropical sprue.

units.title: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
units.sec: Post-Mucosal Phase & Types of Fatty Acids
units.guide:
LCFA + glycerol → esterification → chylomicrons → intestinal lymphatics.
Disorders: abetalipoproteinaemia and intestinal lymphangiectasia.
Chain length >12 / 8-12 / <8; only long chain needs lipolysis and micelles; short chain is colonic and substantial in stool.

units.title: Carbohydrate Absorption Mechanism
units.guide:
Disaccharidases on the brush border: lactase, maltase, sucrase, trehalase.
Gut: SGLT1 (active) for glucose/galactose, GLUT5 for fructose.
Liver: GLUT2 entry then galactokinase, fructokinase, glucokinase.

units.title: Defects in Carbohydrate Absorption
units.guide:
Congenital forms are autosomal recessive.
Selective = lactase deficiency; global = small intestinal mucosal defect (coeliac, Whipple's, tropical sprue).
Primary (m/c) lactase deficiency is allele persistence; secondary follows infections and IBS.

units.title: Protein Absorption & Selective Defects
units.guide:
Trypsinogen → trypsin → activates chymotrypsin and elastase.
Selective defects: enterokinase deficiency, Hartnup's disease (pellagra), cystinuria (COLA).
COLA = cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine.

units.title: Lactose Intolerance: Physiology to Pathogenesis
units.guide:
Lactose (milk, cheese) → lactase (brush border) → glucose + galactose.
Congenital autosomal recessive versus acquired ↓ activity (primary allele persistence, secondary infections/IBS).
Unabsorbed carbohydrate is fermented to acid and H2, methane, CO2.

units.title: Lactose Intolerance: Presentation & Investigations
units.guide:
90 min post prandial distension, bloating, cramps; acidic diaper dermatitis in children.
Stool pH acidic; lactose hydrogen breath test positive at H2 > 20 ppm.
Lactose-glucose blood test is obsolete; treat with diet and calcium.

units.title: Abetalipoproteinemia
units.guide:
AKA neuroacanthocytosis; autosomal recessive; apoB48 → defective esterification → no chylomicrons.
Triad: ataxia (vitamin E), retinitis pigmentosa, steatorrhea; smear shows acanthocytes.
Post prandial endoscopic biopsy is 100% diagnostic with enterocyte vacuolation.

units.title: Intestinal Lymphangiectasia
units.guide:
Chylomicrons cross intestinal lymphatics into blood.
Primary = dilated channels; secondary = lymphoma or Crohn's with lymphatic obstruction.
Protein losing enteropathy with fecal α-1 antitrypsin elevated; treat with medium chain triglyceride diet.
